nuyarn.origin: Nuyarn is a proprietary yarn-construction technology, not a fiber, and the name is a trademark. It is marketed mainly for yarns that combine merino wool from the domestic sheep, Ovis aries, with a continuous synthetic filament, typically a polyamide (nylon), so the generic fibers are usually wool and nylon. Public, independently verifiable information on the owning company, its manufacturing sites and its licensing arrangements is limited, and this entry could not confirm those details from primary sources; the producer's own site is the starting point for such questions.
nuyarn.structure: The fiber chemistry is simply that of the components. Merino wool is alpha-keratin: helical protein chains cross-linked by cystine disulfide bonds, organized into orthocortical and paracortical cells inside an overlapping cuticle of scales, with fine merino commonly in the high teens to low twenties of microns. Nylon filament is an aliphatic polyamide whose chains are held together by amide hydrogen bonds. What the technology changes, according to its marketing, is how the staple wool is arranged around and held by the filament, not the structure of either fiber.
nuyarn.process: Conventional wool yarns rely on twist to bind staple fibers, and twist compacts the yarn. Nuyarn is marketed as an alternative in which drafted wool fibers are assembled around a continuous filament core with little or no twist, relying on the filament for strength so that the wool can stay lofty. The precise machinery and settings are proprietary and could not be verified here. Knitting, dyeing and finishing then follow normal wool-blend practice, and the chosen chemistry must suit both the keratin and the polyamide.
nuyarn.performance: Performance should be judged from fabric test reports rather than from the yarn name. In principle, lower twist can increase bulk and trapped air, which affects warmth, drying time and hand, while a nylon core adds tensile strength and abrasion resistance. Wool contributes high moisture regain, charring and self-extinguishing flame behavior and susceptibility to felting and to clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae; nylon melts rather than chars. Claims about faster drying, stretch or durability are producer statements tied to particular comparisons and constructions.
nuyarn.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) on separated components show wool burning slowly with a burnt-hair odor and crushable ash, and nylon melting to a hard bead. Microscopy reveals scaled wool fibers laid around smooth synthetic filaments. Quantitative blend analysis uses selective dissolution of one component. No laboratory method identifies the Nuyarn brand itself; confusion arises when the name is treated as a fiber, or when a wool and nylon yarn is described as pure merino.
nuyarn.labeling: Nuyarn is a trademark for a yarn technology, not a generic fiber name, so a label must still state the fibers and percentages, for example wool and nylon. In the US, wool content falls under the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 and FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 300, and other fibers under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and 16 CFR Part 303. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires the listed names, such as wool and polyamide or nylon. Any wool-sourcing certification is a separate claim to verify.
nuyarn.past: Nuyarn belongs to a longer history of efforts to change how wool yarn is built rather than which fiber is used: core-spun, wrap-spun and low-twist yarns have long been developed to add strength or bulk. The technology is promoted mainly to outdoor and performance apparel brands for merino base layers, socks and midlayers. Company founding dates, inventors and ownership could not be verified from primary sources in this pass, so they are omitted rather than guessed.
facts: Yarn construction technology (trademark), not a fiber
merino wool with a synthetic filament such as nylon

zq.origin: ZQ is a wool sourcing and assurance program associated with New Zealand merino growers and the brands that buy from them. It is not a sheep breed, species or generic fiber: the fiber is wool, most commonly merino wool from the domestic sheep, Ovis aries. The program sets standards for participating farms and traces wool through the supply chain. This entry could not verify the operating company, launch date or current standard version from primary sources, so readers should consult the program's own documentation for those details.
zq.structure: ZQ does not change fiber structure. Merino wool is alpha-keratin, a protein whose helical chains are cross-linked by cystine disulfide bonds and organized into orthocortical and paracortical cells that produce natural crimp. The surface carries overlapping cuticle scales that cause directional friction and felting, and a thin covalently bound lipid layer makes the surface mildly water-repellent while the interior absorbs moisture. Fine merino is commonly in the high teens to low twenties of microns, but a program label does not specify micron.
zq.process: Wool under any sourcing program follows the usual route: shearing, skirting and classing on farm, baling, then scouring to remove grease, suint and dirt, followed by carding and combing into top for worsted yarns (or carding alone for the woollen route), spinning, and knitting or weaving. A sourcing program adds farm-level auditing, grower agreements and traceability documentation to these steps. The specific audit protocol, frequency and chain-of-custody rules should be taken from ZQ's current standard.
zq.performance: Performance is that of the wool specification, not the program. Merino has high moisture regain among common textile fibers, absorbing water vapor into the keratin with a heat of sorption; good elastic recovery from its crimp; charring and self-extinguishing flame behavior; and susceptibility to felting under heat, moisture and agitation unless shrink-resist treated. It dyes with acid, metal-complex and reactive dyes that bind to amino groups. Keratin is attacked by clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae, and prolonged UV exposure causes yellowing.
zq.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show wool burning slowly with a burnt-hair odor and crushable black ash. Microscopy shows cuticle scale patterns, and laboratory diameter measurement can confirm micron. No laboratory method proves that wool came from a ZQ farm; that depends on program documentation and certificates. A common confusion is treating ZQ as a fiber type or as a guarantee of a particular fineness.
zq.labeling: ZQ is a program trademark, not a generic fiber name, so labels must still state wool and its percentage. In the US, wool labeling is governed by the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 and FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 300; in the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires the name wool for sheep's fleece. Buyers comparing ZQ with other schemes, such as Textile Exchange's Responsible Wool Standard, should compare the published standards, including each scheme's position on mulesing, and confirm certificate scope for the product.
zq.past: Wool sourcing programs grew as brands responded to concerns about animal welfare, particularly flystrike prevention and mulesing in merino flocks, and to demand for traceable, farm-level supply. ZQ emerged in this context from New Zealand merino supply chains, linking growers with apparel and outdoor brands through farm standards and supply agreements. Because the program's history, ownership and standard revisions could not be verified from primary sources in this pass, specific dates and organizational details are omitted rather than guessed.
facts: Wool sourcing and assurance program (trademark), not a fiber
Consult the current ZQ standard and certificates
